prompt: Both x and y hold 7. Is the comparison x < y true?
optionA: Yes, because the values are equal
optionB: No, because the values are equal and < excludes equality
optionC: Yes, because < allows the two to be the same
optionD: It cannot be decided; equal values have no ordering
correctAnswerText: No, because the values are equal and < excludes equality
explanation: A strict comparison asks whether one value is genuinely below the other, and equal values are not. Swapping to <= would make it true, which is exactly the difference between the two operators.

prompt: A queue admits someone when position <= limit. Both position and limit hold 7. Is that person admitted?
optionA: No, because neither of the two is below the other
optionB: No, because <= requires the left-hand value to be the smaller
optionC: It cannot be settled until the two values differ
optionD: Yes, because the two are equal and <= includes equality
correctAnswerText: Yes, because the two are equal and <= includes equality
explanation: The operator holds when the left-hand value is below the right or equal to it, and here the second case applies, so the person is admitted. The strict form would refuse them on exactly the same numbers.

prompt: Both a and b hold 4. What does the comparison a == b produce?
optionA: true
optionC: It stores 4 in a
optionD: An error, because == is not an assignment
correctAnswerText: true
explanation: A double equals asks whether two values are the same and answers true or false. A single equals would store rather than compare, which is the distinction the two symbols exist to keep apart.

prompt: Both m and n hold 10. Is the comparison m != n true?
optionA: Yes, because the names are different
optionB: Yes, because != is true whenever two names are compared
optionC: No, because the values are the same
optionD: It cannot be decided without knowing the type
correctAnswerText: No, because the values are the same
explanation: The comparison is about the values held, not the names holding them. Two different names can perfectly well hold the same value, and here they do.

prompt: A threshold is 18 and the value being checked is exactly 18. Which of these comparisons is false?
optionA: value >= threshold
optionB: value > threshold
optionC: value == threshold
optionD: value <= threshold
correctAnswerText: value > threshold
explanation: At exactly the threshold, every comparison that includes equality holds and the one strict comparison does not. This is why the boundary is the only place the operators can be told apart.

prompt: A program evaluates the comparison 5 > 3. What kind of value does it produce?
optionA: The number 5
optionB: The number 3
optionC: The text "5 > 3"
optionD: A true-or-false value
correctAnswerText: A true-or-false value
explanation: A comparison answers a question, and the answer is one of two values. Neither operand is the result, and nothing about the comparison is kept as text.

prompt: A program runs result = (4 > 2). What does result hold afterwards?
optionA: true
optionD: Nothing; a comparison cannot be stored in a variable
correctAnswerText: true
explanation: The comparison is worked out first and its answer is stored, exactly as any other value would be. Storing the answer to a question is ordinary, and it is what lets a condition be decided once and used later.

prompt: Which of these is a true-or-false value rather than text?
optionA: "true"
optionB: "True"
optionC: true
optionD: "false"
correctAnswerText: true
explanation: The quoted forms are pieces of text that happen to spell the words. Text is never empty and so behaves as true in a condition regardless of what it spells, which makes the quoted version of false particularly misleading.

prompt: A program runs flag = (2 > 9) and then tests if flag:. Does the body run?
optionA: Yes, because flag holds a value and so is true
optionB: No, because the comparison produced false and that is what flag holds
optionC: Yes, because the comparison was successfully carried out
optionD: No, because a stored comparison cannot be tested again
correctAnswerText: No, because the comparison produced false and that is what flag holds
explanation: What flag holds is the answer to the comparison, not the fact that a comparison happened. The comparison ran perfectly well and produced false; testing that stored answer is exactly the point of keeping it.

prompt: A fragment reads: if x > 0: / [indented] print("A") / print("B"), where only the first print is indented. Which lines run when x is 5?
optionA: Only the first print runs
optionB: Only the second print runs
optionC: Neither runs, because the second is outside the conditional
optionD: Both prints run
correctAnswerText: Both prints run
explanation: The indented line belongs to the conditional and runs because the condition held; the unindented line sits after the conditional and runs regardless. Both therefore run here.

prompt: The same fragment reads: if x > 0: / [indented] print("A") / print("B"). Which lines run when x is -5?
optionA: Only the second print runs
optionB: Neither runs
optionC: Both run
optionD: Only the first print runs
correctAnswerText: Only the second print runs
explanation: The condition fails, so the indented line is skipped, but the unindented line was never part of the conditional and runs anyway. Reading it as part of the branch is the misreading this measures.

prompt: In a fragment with an if branch and an else branch, how many of the two branches run on any single pass?
optionA: Both, in the order written
optionB: Neither, unless the condition is stored first
optionC: Exactly one
optionD: It depends on how many lines each branch contains
correctAnswerText: Exactly one
explanation: The condition selects one branch and the other is skipped entirely. Neither the length of the branches nor anything stored beforehand changes that.

prompt: A fragment reads: if x > 0: / [indented] print("A") / else: / [indented] print("B") / print("C"). How many lines of output appear for any value of x?
optionA: One, whichever branch is chosen
optionB: Two: one from the chosen branch, and C
optionC: Three, since every print is reached
optionD: Two: A and B, with C only when the condition holds
correctAnswerText: Two: one from the chosen branch, and C
explanation: One branch runs and the other does not, so the branches contribute exactly one line between them; the unindented line after the conditional then always runs. The total is the same whatever x holds.

prompt: A program sets balance = 500 and price = 450, then sets price = 500, then tests balance >= price. Does the condition hold?
optionA: No; the two are now equal, and the operator needs the left value to be larger
optionB: Yes; it is checked against 450, the value price held first
optionC: No; a comparison of two equal values produces neither answer
optionD: Yes; the two are now equal, and the operator includes equality
correctAnswerText: Yes; the two are now equal, and the operator includes equality
explanation: A condition looks at what the names hold when it runs, which here is 500 on both sides. The earlier 450 has been replaced and plays no part, and equal values are handled by whether the operator admits equality.

prompt: A program sets stock = 3 and then tests stock > 5. Does the condition hold?
optionA: No; 3 is not above 5
optionB: Yes; the comparison is read as 5 being above 3
optionC: Yes; stock holds a value, so the check passes
optionD: It cannot be decided without a second value to compare against
correctAnswerText: No; 3 is not above 5
explanation: The name on the left is the one being asked about, so the question is whether 3 exceeds 5. Reading the comparison in the other direction is the commonest way to get the answer exactly backwards.

prompt: A program sets total = 20, then total = total - 8, then tests total < 15. Does the condition hold?
optionA: No; total holds 20 when the test runs
optionB: No; 12 is not below 15
optionC: Yes; total holds 12 by the time the test runs
optionD: Yes; but only because the subtraction happens again during the test
correctAnswerText: Yes; total holds 12 by the time the test runs
explanation: The subtraction has already replaced what total holds, so the test sees 12 and 12 is below 15. Evaluating against the original 20 is the slip; nothing is recomputed while the condition is checked.

prompt: A fragment reads: IF marks >= 40 PRINT "Pass" ELSE PRINT "Fail". The marks are 75. What is printed?
optionA: Fail
optionB: Pass
optionC: Both Pass and Fail
optionD: Nothing, because the condition only checks and does not print
correctAnswerText: Pass
explanation: 75 satisfies the condition, so the first branch runs and the second is skipped entirely. Only one of the two branches can ever print, and one of them always does.

prompt: A fragment reads: IF stock > 0 PRINT "Available" ELSE PRINT "Out of stock". The stock is 0. What is printed?
optionA: Available
optionB: Both Available and Out of stock
optionC: Nothing, because 0 is neither above nor below the threshold
optionD: Out of stock
correctAnswerText: Out of stock
explanation: A strict comparison excludes the boundary, so a stock of 0 fails the condition and the else branch runs. The boundary is always handled by one branch or the other; it is never left undecided.

prompt: A fragment reads: IF age >= 18 PRINT "Eligible" ELSE PRINT "Not Eligible", and then, outside the conditional, PRINT "Done". The age is 20. What is printed?
optionA: Eligible, then Done
optionB: Eligible only
optionC: Eligible, then Not Eligible, then Done
optionD: Done only
correctAnswerText: Eligible, then Done
explanation: The condition selects the first branch, and the line after the conditional was never part of either branch, so it runs as well. Treating that trailing line as belonging to the else is the misreading worth catching.

prompt: A fragment has a single if with no else. The condition is false. What happens?
optionA: The body runs anyway, as a default
optionB: The program stops, because there is nowhere to go
optionC: Nothing in the conditional runs, and the program carries on afterwards
optionD: The program refuses to run, because an if requires an else
correctAnswerText: Nothing in the conditional runs, and the program carries on afterwards
explanation: An if with no else offers one optional branch and nothing more; when the condition fails there is simply nothing to do. An else is optional, and its absence is neither an error nor a reason to run the body.

prompt: A fragment reads: if grade >= 70 print "High"; else if grade >= 50 print "Middle"; else if grade >= 30 print "Low". The grade is 20. What is printed?
optionA: Low, because the last branch catches whatever is left
optionB: Nothing; no condition held and there is no final catch-all
optionC: High, because the first branch is the default
optionD: An error, because no branch matched
correctAnswerText: Nothing; no condition held and there is no final catch-all
explanation: Every branch here carries its own condition, including the last one, so a value below all three matches none of them. A final branch only catches everything when it has no condition attached at all.

prompt: A chain reads: if score >= 90 print "A"; else if score >= 75 print "B"; else print "C". The score is 76. What is printed?
optionA: A
optionB: C
optionC: Both B and C
optionD: B
correctAnswerText: B
explanation: 76 fails the first condition and satisfies the second, so B is printed and the rest of the chain is abandoned. A chain stops at its first true condition rather than testing them all.

prompt: A chain reads: if score >= 75 print "B"; else if score >= 90 print "A"; else print "C". The score is 95. What is printed?
optionA: B, because the first condition it meets is the one written first
optionB: A, because 95 is at least 90
optionC: Both B and A, because 95 satisfies each of them
optionD: C, because the chain has no branch for a score this high
correctAnswerText: B, because the first condition it meets is the one written first
explanation: A score of 95 satisfies both of the first two conditions, and the chain stops at whichever is written earlier. Written in this order the branch for the highest scores can never be reached, which is why order is part of the meaning rather than a matter of style.

prompt: A chain reads: if n > 100 print "big"; else if n > 10 print "medium"; else print "small". Someone swaps the first two branches. The outputs for 5 and for 8 are unchanged, and the output for 200 changes. What does that show?
optionA: The swap broke the final branch, which now catches large values
optionB: Swapping branches never changes behaviour, so the difference must come from elsewhere
optionC: Values above 100 also satisfy the condition for medium, so after the swap they reach it first
optionD: Both branches now run for large values
correctAnswerText: Values above 100 also satisfy the condition for medium, so after the swap they reach it first
explanation: The two conditions overlap, and the outputs that stayed the same are the ones no overlap touches. Only a value satisfying both can reveal the order, which is why the small values were unaffected while 200 was not.

prompt: Entry requires an identity card and a permission slip. Someone has the card but no permission slip. May they enter?
optionA: Yes; and is satisfied as soon as one part holds
optionB: No; and requires both parts, and one is missing
optionC: Yes; the card is the stronger of the two requirements
optionD: It cannot be decided without knowing which requirement matters more
correctAnswerText: No; and requires both parts, and one is missing
explanation: A combined requirement joined by and fails as soon as any part fails, regardless of how important the parts seem. Treating one satisfied part as enough is what or would mean.

prompt: A discount applies if age < 18 or age > 60. The age is 65. Does the discount apply?
optionA: No; 65 fails the first part, so the whole condition fails
optionB: No; or requires both parts to hold
optionC: It cannot be decided, because the two parts disagree
optionD: Yes; or needs only one part to hold, and 65 is above 60
correctAnswerText: Yes; or needs only one part to hold, and 65 is above 60
explanation: A condition joined by or holds as soon as any part holds, so failing the first part settles nothing on its own. Requiring both parts is what and would mean, and parts disagreeing is the ordinary case rather than an obstacle.

prompt: A user is blocked when not (verified and active). A particular user is verified but is not active. Is that user blocked?
optionA: Yes; the combined condition fails, so its negation holds
optionB: No; the user is verified, so the negation does not apply
optionC: No; not applies only to the first part, and the user is verified
optionD: Yes; not makes any condition true
correctAnswerText: Yes; the combined condition fails, so its negation holds
explanation: The inner condition needs both parts and only one holds, so it is false and negating it gives true. Being verified would matter if not attached to that part alone, and it does not — the brackets place it over the whole combination.

prompt: A student passes when marks >= 40. The marks are exactly 40. What is the result?
optionA: Fail, because 40 does not exceed 40
optionB: Pass, but only once the mark is raised above 40
optionC: Pass
optionD: Nothing is decided, because the value sits on the boundary
correctAnswerText: Pass
explanation: The operator includes equality, so the boundary value itself satisfies the rule. A value sitting exactly on a threshold is always decided by whether the operator admits equality, never left undecided.

prompt: A fragment reads: IF temp > 40 PRINT "Alert" ELSE PRINT "Normal". The temperature is exactly 40. What is printed?
optionA: Alert
optionB: Normal
optionC: Nothing, since 40 is neither above nor below the threshold
optionD: An error, because the boundary value is not covered by either branch
correctAnswerText: Normal
explanation: A strict comparison excludes the boundary, so 40 fails the condition and the else branch runs. The boundary is always covered — by the else — which is precisely why the choice of operator decides which side it lands on.

prompt: A rule says a student passes with a mark of at least 40, but the code tests marks > 40. Every mark it was tried on gave the right result. Which input does it get wrong?
optionA: A mark of 100
optionB: Any mark below 40
optionC: Every mark above 40
optionD: A mark of exactly 40
correctAnswerText: A mark of exactly 40
explanation: The two conditions agree on every value except the one where they differ, which is the threshold itself. That is why testing with ordinary marks — well above or well below — could never have revealed it.

prompt: A fragment reads: if a > 0: / [indented] if b > 0: / [twice indented] print("both") / [indented] else: / [twice indented] print("first only"). With a = 5 and b = -1, what is printed?
optionA: first only
optionB: both
optionC: Nothing
optionD: both, then first only
correctAnswerText: first only
explanation: The outer condition holds, so the inner conditional is reached; the inner condition fails, so its else runs. Only one branch of the inner conditional can run, and it is reached only because the outer one held.

prompt: The same nested fragment is run with a = -5 and b = 9. Nothing at all is printed, even though b satisfies the inner condition. Why?
optionA: The inner condition was evaluated but its result was discarded
optionB: The inner else ran and printed nothing
optionC: The inner conditional is never reached, because the outer condition failed
optionD: A negative value in the outer condition stops the fragment entirely
correctAnswerText: The inner conditional is never reached, because the outer condition failed
explanation: An inner conditional is part of the outer branch, so it is only considered when the outer condition holds. That b would have satisfied it is exactly the point: it was never asked.

prompt: A fragment is meant to print "low" whenever a is not positive. It reads: if a > 0: / [indented] if b > 0: / [twice indented] print("ok") / [indented] else: / [twice indented] print("low"). It prints nothing for negative values of a, and prints low for some positive ones. What is wrong?
optionA: The outer condition should test a < 0 instead
optionB: The else is attached to the inner conditional, so it is only reached when a is positive
optionC: The two branches were written in the wrong order
optionD: The inner condition should test b < 0
correctAnswerText: The else is attached to the inner conditional, so it is only reached when a is positive
explanation: The pattern of failures identifies the fault: low appearing for positive values of a shows the else belongs to the inner test, and nothing appearing for negative values shows the outer branch has no else at all. Indentation is what decides which conditional an else joins.

prompt: A rule says: a passenger travels free if they are under 5 years old. Which condition implements it exactly?
optionA: age <= 5
optionB: age > 5
optionC: age <= 4
optionD: age < 5
correctAnswerText: age < 5
explanation: "Under 5" excludes 5 itself, so the strict comparison is the one that matches. The inclusive version admits a five-year-old, and the version stopping at 4 happens to agree for whole years but not for an age recorded with months.

prompt: A rule says: a discount applies at a quantity of at least 12. A condition was written that behaves correctly for every quantity tested, and the quantities tested were 5, 8, 20 and 30. Which condition might still be wrong?
optionA: quantity > 12, which excludes 12 itself
optionB: quantity >= 12, which is what the rule states
optionC: quantity > 11, which admits every quantity of 12 or more
optionD: quantity >= 11.5, which admits every whole quantity of 12 or more
correctAnswerText: quantity > 12, which excludes 12 itself
explanation: None of the quantities tested is 12, so any condition that differs only at 12 would pass all four. The strict comparison is exactly such a condition; the other two, although written oddly, admit 12 and therefore match the rule for whole quantities.

prompt: A rule says: charge extra when the weight is more than 20 kg. Two candidate conditions are weight > 20 and weight >= 20. A parcel weighing exactly 20 kg was charged extra, which is wrong. Which condition was used, and what should replace it?
optionA: weight > 20 was used; it should be weight >= 20
optionB: Either could have been used; the fault is elsewhere
optionC: weight >= 20 was used; it should be weight > 20
optionD: weight >= 20 was used, and it is correct; the rule is what needs changing
correctAnswerText: weight >= 20 was used; it should be weight > 20
explanation: "More than" excludes the value itself, so a parcel at exactly the threshold should not be charged. That it was charged shows the inclusive operator was used, and only a value sitting exactly on the boundary could have told the two apart.

prompt: Login should succeed only when the username and the password are both correct. The code joins the two checks with or, and it admits anyone who gets the username right with the wrong password. What is the fault?
optionA: The password check is missing altogether
optionB: The two checks should be joined with and, since or succeeds when either part holds
optionC: The two checks are written in the wrong order
optionD: The joining is correct, and the password comparison is reversed
correctAnswerText: The two checks should be joined with and, since or succeeds when either part holds
explanation: The failing cases are precisely those where one check passes and the other does not, which is the behaviour of or and not of and. A missing check would admit everyone, and order does not affect whether a combined condition holds.

prompt: A fragment should report "valid" when a value lies between 10 and 20 inclusive. It reports valid for 15, and also for 5 and for 25. What is the fault?
optionA: The comparisons exclude the boundaries 10 and 20
optionB: The comparisons are reversed, so the range runs the wrong way
optionC: The value is being compared as text rather than as a number
optionD: The two parts are joined with or, so a value outside the range still satisfies one of them
correctAnswerText: The two parts are joined with or, so a value outside the range still satisfies one of them
explanation: A value below the range and a value above it both being accepted is the signature of or: 5 is below 20 and 25 is above 10, so each satisfies one half. A boundary fault would show only at 10 and 20, and reversed comparisons would reject 15 as well.

prompt: A fragment classifies values as "in range" or "out of range" for a range of 1 to 100. It behaves correctly on every value between 1 and 100 and on every value above 100, but calls every negative value in range. Which single fault produces exactly that pattern?
optionA: Only the upper limit is checked, so anything at or below 100 is accepted
optionB: Only the lower limit is checked, so anything at or above 1 is accepted
optionC: The two limits are swapped, so the range runs from 100 down to 1
optionD: The boundaries are excluded, so 1 and 100 are rejected
correctAnswerText: Only the upper limit is checked, so anything at or below 100 is accepted
explanation: Working backwards from which inputs fail: negatives accepted means nothing enforces a floor, and values above 100 correctly rejected means the ceiling is enforced. Checking only the lower limit would produce the opposite pattern, and swapped limits would reject everything.

prompt: A fragment awards a bonus when sales are above target and returns are below a limit. It has never awarded a bonus to anyone, although several people have met both conditions. Which fault explains an outcome that never happens at all?
optionA: The conditions were joined with or instead of and
optionB: The target is set slightly too high
optionC: The two conditions were joined so that they can never both hold, such as requiring returns to be both below and above the limit
optionD: The bonus is awarded in the branch that runs, but the amount is zero
correctAnswerText: The two conditions were joined so that they can never both hold, such as requiring returns to be both below and above the limit
explanation: A rule that never fires, on data that should fire it, is different in kind from a rule that fires too often or too rarely: it points at a condition that cannot be satisfied rather than one set wrongly. Joining with or would award too many bonuses, and a target set too high would still let someone through eventually.

prompt: A conditional gives the wrong answer for exactly one input out of thousands, and right answers for all the rest. Compared with one that is wrong for half its inputs, which is harder to find, and why?
optionA: The one wrong for half its inputs, because so much output has to be checked
optionB: The one wrong for a single input, because ordinary testing is unlikely to include that input
optionC: They are equally hard, since both are wrong
optionD: The one wrong for a single input, because the fault must be larger to hide so well
correctAnswerText: The one wrong for a single input, because ordinary testing is unlikely to include that input
explanation: A fault affecting half the inputs shows up in almost any test; one affecting a single value survives every test that does not happen to use it, which is why boundaries are tested deliberately rather than sampled. Rarity of a symptom says nothing about the size of the mistake behind it.

prompt: A chain reads: if n > 10 print "A"; else if n > 50 print "B"; else print "C". In months of use, B has never once been printed. Why?
optionA: Values above 50 are rare in the data
optionB: B is only reachable when n is exactly 50
optionC: The chain is correct; B must be printed sometimes
optionD: Every value above 50 is also above 10, so the first branch always takes it
correctAnswerText: Every value above 50 is also above 10, so the first branch always takes it
explanation: The second condition is stricter than the first and comes after it, so nothing can ever reach it. This is a property of the chain rather than of the data — no input whatsoever prints B.

prompt: A chain reads: if age >= 18 print "adult"; else if age >= 65 print "senior"; else print "minor". Which branch can never run, and what single change makes the chain behave as its labels suggest?
optionA: The senior branch; putting the age of 65 test before the age of 18 test makes all three reachable
optionB: The minor branch; it should be tested first
optionC: None; each branch runs for some age
optionD: The adult branch; it should test a range rather than a floor
correctAnswerText: The senior branch; putting the age of 65 test before the age of 18 test makes all three reachable
explanation: Everyone at 65 or above is also 18 or above, so the earlier branch claims them. Ordering the conditions from the most demanding to the least is what makes a chain of overlapping thresholds work, and it needs no extra conditions.

prompt: A chain tests three conditions that do not overlap at all — for example equality against three different values. Can any of its branches be unreachable through ordering alone?
optionA: Yes; the last branch is always unreachable in a chain of three
optionB: Yes; whichever condition is written last becomes unreachable
optionC: No; with no overlap, no earlier condition can claim a value a later one would have matched
optionD: It cannot be determined without knowing the values
correctAnswerText: No; with no overlap, no earlier condition can claim a value a later one would have matched
explanation: Unreachability through ordering requires one condition to cover values another would have matched, and disjoint conditions never do. Order still decides which test runs first, but not whether any branch can be reached.

prompt: A chain reads: if x >= 0 print "non-negative"; else if x > -1 print "small negative"; else print "negative". On whole numbers, is the middle branch reachable?
optionA: No, under any values at all
optionB: No on whole numbers, but yes once fractions are allowed, where a value such as -0.5 reaches it
optionC: Yes; -1 itself reaches it
optionD: Yes; every negative value reaches it
correctAnswerText: No on whole numbers, but yes once fractions are allowed, where a value such as -0.5 reaches it
explanation: The middle branch needs a value below 0 and above -1, and no whole number lies there. Widening the type opens the gap, so reachability is a claim about the values a program will actually see, not about the text alone. The value -1 satisfies neither of the first two conditions.

prompt: A team finds that one branch of a long chain is unreachable. One person wants to delete it; another wants to reorder the chain so it can run. How should the choice be made?
optionA: By deleting it, since unreachable code is always waste
optionB: By reordering, since a branch someone wrote must have been wanted
optionC: By leaving it, since removing code risks changing behaviour
optionD: By deciding whether the branch describes a case that should be handled; deleting is right only if it should not
correctAnswerText: By deciding whether the branch describes a case that should be handled; deleting is right only if it should not
explanation: Unreachability is a symptom, and the two remedies mean opposite things: one says the case does not exist, the other says the chain fails to handle a case that does. Deleting silently settles that question without anyone deciding it.

prompt: Two conditions, x > 0 and x >= 1, were tried on whole numbers from 2 to 50 and agreed on every one. Are they equivalent for all the values this program can receive, given that it also accepts 0 and negative whole numbers?
optionA: Yes for whole numbers, including 0 and negatives, since no whole number lies between 0 and 1
optionB: No; they differ at 0
optionC: No; they differ for every negative value
optionD: No; they differ at 1
correctAnswerText: Yes for whole numbers, including 0 and negatives, since no whole number lies between 0 and 1
explanation: At 0 both are false, at 1 both are true, and below 0 both are false, so on whole numbers the two select exactly the same values. The range tested was too narrow to establish that, but widening it to the values actually accepted still finds no difference.

prompt: Is the condition not (a and b) the same as (not a) or (not b), for every combination of true and false?
optionA: No; they differ when both a and b are true
optionB: No; they differ when both a and b are false
optionC: Yes; they agree on all four combinations
optionD: Yes, but only when a and b are never both false
correctAnswerText: Yes; they agree on all four combinations
explanation: Negating a requirement for both parts gives a requirement that either part is missing, which is what the second condition says. Checking all four combinations settles it outright: with only two inputs, every case can be examined rather than sampled.

prompt: Is the condition not (a and b) the same as (not a) and (not b)?
optionA: Yes; negation applies to each part in turn
optionB: No; they differ whenever exactly one of a and b holds
optionC: No; they differ only when both hold
optionD: No; they differ only when neither holds
correctAnswerText: No; they differ whenever exactly one of a and b holds
explanation: With one part true and one false, the combined requirement fails so its negation is true, while the second condition needs both parts to be missing and so is false. When both hold or neither does, the two agree — which is why a careless check that tries only those two cases finds nothing wrong.

prompt: Two conditions select exactly the same values, but one is a single comparison and the other is four comparisons joined together. On what grounds should the choice between them be made?
optionA: On neither; conditions selecting the same values are interchangeable
optionB: On which was written first
optionC: On the longer one, since more comparisons cover more cases
optionD: On which states the underlying rule more directly, since correctness no longer separates them
correctAnswerText: On which states the underlying rule more directly, since correctness no longer separates them
explanation: Once two conditions agree on every input, nothing about behaviour distinguishes them and what remains is whether the next person can see the rule in the code. More comparisons cover no more cases here — that is precisely what equivalence means.
